claims.text: Structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is primarily governed by configurational entropy of mixing.
Configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation relative to lower-entropy alloys.
Configurational entropy suppresses atomic diffusion relative to lower-entropy alloys.
The proposed initial material is a uniformly composed and structured, equiatomic five-element nanoalloy.
The proposed intervention is extended exposure at 800–1000°C under an inert atmosphere.
The controlled comparison uses a binary or ternary low-entropy nanoalloy of similar size and initial structure under identical heating conditions.
High configurational entropy increases the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
Increasing the barrier for atomic rearrangement inhibits phase separation.
The proposed entropy-mediated mechanism stabilizes a single-phase structure against thermally driven segregation.
The proposed entropy-mediated mechanism preserves a homogeneous chemical distribution during heating.
The proposed entropy-mediated mechanism suppresses thermally driven coarsening.
After high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a single-phase, compositionally homogeneous structure.
Under the same exposure, low-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit phase segregation, grain growth, or compositional inhomogeneity.
Differences in phase state, morphology, and elemental homogeneity can be observed using XRD, TEM, and EDS mapping.
The prediction is limited to near-equiatomic nanoalloys with at least five principal elements, particle sizes below 100 nm, temperatures up to 1000°C, and inert atmospheres.
Extreme element combinations or reactive atmospheres may cause deviations from the prediction.
The magnitude of stability enhancement may depend on the selected elements and synthesis method.
The prediction assumes ideal mixing and no strong inter-element immiscibility.
Comparable or greater segregation, grain growth, or compositional inhomogeneity in the high-entropy material relative to the low-entropy control would falsify the hypothesis.
